issues.legal_issue: An acquiring authority that is aggrieved by a compensation award may appeal even if it was not impleaded in the compensation reference.
material_facts: The acquiring authority was not impleaded before the Reference Court and had no opportunity to adduce evidence there.
The acquiring authority challenged the compensation award before the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The acquiring authority was a person aggrieved and its appeal under Section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act was maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act permits an appeal by a person aggrieved by the award; the acquiring authority's status as an aggrieved person is not defeated merely because it was not impleaded in the reference proceedings.

predicates.acquiring_authority_aggrieved_by_award: The authority responsible for the acquisition was adversely affected by the compensation award.
predicates.award_made_without_authority_as_party: The compensation award was made in proceedings in which the acquiring authority was not a party.
predicates.acquiring_authority_appeals: The acquiring authority appealed against the compensation award.

issues.definition: When an acquiring authority is adversely affected by an award made without it as a party, its appeal against that award is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land must be determined by assessing relevant comparable-sale evidence, and a valuation based solely on witness testimony or prior awards while ignoring available sale deeds is legally flawed.
material_facts: The Collector considered sale deeds from nearby land transactions and assessed the market value at a lower rate.
The Reference Court relied on a witness's account of the land's fertility and development and on awards in other acquisition cases to enhance compensation.
The Reference Court ignored the sale deeds considered by the Collector, and the acquiring authority challenged that approach.
The High Court dismissed the acquiring authority's appeals without correcting the Reference Court's approach.
issues.conclusion: The Reference Court erred by relying solely on the witness's testimony and prior awards while ignoring the sale deeds; it was required to assess comparable sales and give sufficient, cogent reasons if it differed from the Collector's assessment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, market value is assessed by reference to what a willing purchaser would pay. Comparable sales are generally preferred and must be assessed for genuineness, temporal and geographical proximity, similarity of the land, and comparability of plot size; adjustments may be made for differences. Prior judgments and awards have evidentiary value, particularly in the absence of better evidence. The Court relied on Shaji Kuriakose v. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. (2001) 7 SCC 650, P. Ram Reddy v. Land Acquisition Officer (1995) 2 SCC 305, Panna Lal Ghosh v. Land Acquisition Collector (2004) 1 SCC 467, and Viluben Jhalejar Contractor v. State of Gujarat (2005) 4 SCC 789.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and sale_deeds_available and sale_deeds_ignored and valuation_based_only_on_testimony_or_prior_awards

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns the amount of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.sale_deeds_available: Relevant sale deeds concerning potentially comparable land were available to the decision-maker.
predicates.sale_deeds_ignored: The decision-maker did not consider the available sale deeds when determining market value.
predicates.valuation_based_only_on_testimony_or_pri: The decision-maker based the valuation only on witness testimony or awards from other acquisition cases.

issues.definition: In a land-acquisition compensation case, ignoring available sale deeds and valuing the land only by testimony or prior awards makes the valuation method legally flawed.

issues.legal_issue: A court hearing an appeal from a compensation award must assess the relevant factual and legal issues rather than dismiss the appeal without properly examining them.
material_facts: The acquiring authority's appeal challenged the Reference Court's reliance on testimony and its failure to consider sale deeds.
The High Court dismissed the appeals by relying on evidence of an award in another acquisition case, without adequately addressing the challenged valuation approach.
issues.conclusion: The High Court failed to address the correct questions and relevant facts, misdirected itself in law, and was wrong to dismiss the appeals in that manner.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal under Section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act, the appellate court must consider both the factual and legal aspects of the case, including the applicable compensation principles and relevant evidence.

predicates.first_appeal_from_compensation_award: The proceeding is an appeal from a compensation award.
predicates.appeal_challenges_facts_or_law: The appellant challenges factual or legal aspects of the compensation decision.
predicates.appellate_court_dismisses_without_assess: The appellate court dismisses the appeal without properly considering the relevant evidence and issues raised.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a compensation award raises factual or legal challenges, dismissing it without assessing the relevant evidence and issues is inadequate appellate review.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may decline discretionary appellate relief despite identifying legal errors when the circumstances do not warrant interference.
material_facts: The Supreme Court identified errors in the Reference Court's valuation and in the High Court's review.
The amount in dispute in each appeal was small compared with the likely cost of further litigation.
The acquiring authorities had deposited part of the awarded compensation, which the claimants had presumably withdrawn.
Remitting the matters for reconsideration would require both sides to incur substantial further litigation costs.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere in its discretionary jurisdiction and dismissed the appeals despite its findings of error.
issues.legal_principle: The Court may refuse discretionary relief even where an order is legally wrong. It relied on Article 136 of the Constitution and S.D.S. Shipping (P) Ltd. v. Jay Container Services Co. (P) Ltd. (2003) 9 SCC 439, as well as High Court of Judicature at Bombay v. Brij Mohan Gupta (2003) 2 SCC 390, N.K. Prasada v. Government of India (2004) 6 SCC 299, Inder Parkash Gupta v. State of J&K (2004) 6 SCC 786, and Board of Control for Cricket in India v. Netaji Cricket Club (2005) 4 SCC 741. The Court also noted its power under Article 142 to make appropriate orders to do complete justice.

rule.if: supreme_court_discretionary_appeal and lower_court_error_found and amount_at_stake_small and further_litigation_costs_disproportionate

predicates.supreme_court_discretionary_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court invoking its discretionary appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.lower_court_error_found: The Supreme Court identifies an error in the decision under appeal.
predicates.amount_at_stake_small: The financial amount at stake is small in relation to the proceedings.
predicates.further_litigation_costs_disproportionat: Further litigation would impose costs disproportionate to the amount at stake.

issues.definition: Where the Supreme Court finds an error but the amount at stake is small and further litigation costs are disproportionate, it may refuse discretionary appellate relief.
